project.topic: What if 8.3 billion people farted at once?
project.title: What if 8.3 billion people farted at once?
project.audience: International, curious nontechnical viewers of science shorts (13+).
project.core_question: If everyone on Earth farted in the same second, would anyone outside your elevator even notice?
project.viewer_takeaway: Smell depends on how little air it mixes into: a crowded elevator gets several times the detectable dose, open air erases it in steps, and the whole planet’s output is a speck in the atmosphere whose methane cows match in seconds.

scientific_model.baseline_reality: People pass gas about 10 times a day, roughly 35-90 mL each time; it is mostly nitrogen, carbon dioxide, hydrogen and some methane, and its smell comes from traces of sulfur gases such as hydrogen sulfide.
scientific_model.counterfactual_change: All 8.3 billion people pass one ordinary amount of gas (about 60 mL) in the same second. Nothing else changes. The film follows one crowded elevator, a street outside, the planet, and a cattle pasture.
assumptions: One passage per person of about 60 mL (35-90 mL range).
Hydrogen sulfide about 1.06 µmol/L of flatus (about 26 ppm); smell threshold taken as 0.47 ppb (published values range to about 8 ppb).
Six riders in an elevator holding about 5 m³ of air.
The yellow-green tint is a visual stand-in for colourless gas.
causal_chain: Everyone passes gas in the same second.
In a small closed space the sulfur gases reach several times the smell threshold.
In open air a single passage dilutes below smelling range within about 3 m³ of air, a few steps.
Together it is about 500,000 m³, roughly 200 Olympic pools.
Spread through the atmosphere it is about 0.12 parts per trillion.
Its 10-50 t of methane equals what the world’s cattle burp in under half a minute.
uncertainties: Volume, methane and sulfur content vary widely between people and diets.
Air in real elevators exchanges with the shaft, so concentrations fall over minutes.
Smell thresholds vary greatly between people.

claims.statement: The scenario has all 8.3 billion people pass gas in the same second.
claims.reasoning: Stipulated premise; the population is close to the UN estimate for 2026.
claims.presentation_guardrail: The 8.3 billion count is the premise.

claims.statement: Flatus contains about 1.06 µmol/L of hydrogen sulfide, the main contributor to its odour, plus smaller amounts of methanethiol and dimethyl sulfide.

Six passages of about 60 mL in a ~5 m³ elevator raise hydrogen sulfide to about 2 ppb once fully mixed, roughly four times the commonly cited 0.47 ppb smell threshold; before mixing, the plumes around each rider are far stronger.
claims.reasoning: 6 x 0.06 L x 26 ppm / 5,000 L = 1.9 ppb. Published H2S odour thresholds span roughly 0.5-8 ppb; against the higher values the mixed level is below detection, but unmixed plumes near each person (a 60 mL puff spread into 0.5 m³ is about 3 ppb) and the lower-threshold methanethiol keep it smellable in the first minute.
claims.presentation_guardrail: "Several times" refers to the 0.47 ppb threshold; the HUD shows the mixed H2S level.

claims.statement: In open air a single passage (about 26 ppm H2S inside the puff) falls below the 0.47 ppb smell threshold once it has mixed into about 3 m³ of air, roughly a 55,000-fold dilution that a breeze achieves within a few seconds.
claims.reasoning: 60 mL x 26 ppm / 0.47 ppb = about 3.3 m³; outdoor turbulent mixing over a few metres.
claims.presentation_guardrail: One street moment; smell can linger in still air or clothing.

claims.statement: All passages together are about 500,000 m³ of gas, roughly 200 Olympic swimming pools (2,500 m³ each).
claims.reasoning: 8.3e9 x 60 mL; range about 115-300 pools for 35-90 mL.

claims.statement: Mixed into the whole atmosphere (about 4.2e18 m³ at sea-level density), that is about 0.12 parts per trillion, less than one part in five trillion.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Even the largest volumes stay below one part in five trillion.

claims.statement: Flatus methane averages a few to about 15 percent, so everyone’s passage together holds roughly 10-50 tonnes of methane.
claims.reasoning: Methane share varies (a meta-analysis mean of about 14%; many people produce little); 500,000 m³ x 3-15% x 0.66 kg/m³.

claims.statement: The world’s cattle emit roughly 85 Mt of methane a year from digestion, about 2.7 tonnes per second, mostly by burping; they match humanity’s one-second total in under half a minute.
claims.reasoning: Enteric fermentation is about 39% of livestock’s 7.1 Gt CO2-eq (FAO 2013), about 110 Mt CH4/yr, and cattle make about 75% of it.
claims.presentation_guardrail: "Under half a minute" covers the 4-19 s range.

sources.name: Tomlin, Lowis & Read (1991), Investigation of normal flatus production in healthy volunteers, Gut
Suarez, Springfield & Levitt (1998), Identification of gases responsible for the odour of human flatus, Gut
Meta-analysis of the composition of human intestinal gases (2021)
Hydrogen sulfide odour threshold (Public Lab summary of standard data)
Saunois et al. (2020), The global methane budget 2000-2017

creative_direction.logline: Everyone on Earth farts in the same second: your elevator is in trouble, the street is fine, the planet shrugs, and cows do it bigger every few seconds.
creative_direction.visual_identity: Deadpan comedy staged with grounded 3D: a cramped steel elevator of frozen side-eyes, a sunny street, a swelling bubble over the rooftops, a quiet orbit view and a herd of burping cows; the gas shown as a faint tint.
creative_direction.lighting: Cool elevator panel light against a warm lobby; bright midday street and pasture; orbit sun from the right.
creative_direction.camera_language: Handheld eye-level POV in the elevator and on the street; slow orbit pull-backs for scale.
creative_direction.motion_language: Comic timing from stillness: a collective jolt, frozen glances, then small reactions; slow swelling and thinning gas.
creative_direction.world_scale_policy: Metre scale on the ground; Earth radius 1 in orbit; the bubble at true size (98 m); the gas tint exaggerated so it can be seen.
creative_direction.opening_hook: Everyone in your elevator just farted at once. Including you.
creative_direction.mid_video_rehook: Outside on the street it is gone within a few steps; even all 8.3 billion together, 200 Olympic pools of gas, is less than one part in five trillion of the air, and cows out-emit its methane in seconds.
creative_direction.ending_payoff: The planet will not notice; whoever rides this elevator next definitely will.
creative_direction.loop_connection: The film ends where it began, in the same elevator, as its doors open on the next passenger.
creative_direction.asset_policy: Reuse humanoids, street, globe, grass, trees, sky rig and the lit puff system; add a reusable dairy-cow-v1.

audio.voice_style: Crisp, urgent, fascinated adult male; high-tension simulation narrator; brisk opening cadence
audio.music_direction: Original playful score: pizzicato and muted brass stings, a tuba comic rumble for the planet, a light bouncy groove outside, a deflating slide for the speck, and a final ding with a button chord.
audio.sfx_direction: Elevator hum dropping out for a beat before the moment; a comic low blip; awkward sniff and cough; button clicks; street breeze; balloon stretch; deflating squeak; cow burps; elevator ding.

distribution.distinctive_angle: Where you are decides everything: a crowded elevator gets several times the smellable dose, the street erases it, the planet doesn’t notice, and cows out-emit it in seconds.
distribution.comment_bait_question: What’s the worst place on Earth to be at that exact second?
distribution.seo_integrity_note: Comic thought experiment with real numbers: volumes, smell and methane are typical-value estimates; the gas is colourless (the tint is a visual aid).
